claim: Eye and head movements add rotational velocity patterns to the retinal image as we navigate through the world.
source: As we navigate through the world, eye and head movements add rotational velocity patterns to the retinal image.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about how self-motion affects visual input.

claim: When rotations accompany observer translation, the rotational velocity patterns must be discounted to accurately perceive heading.
source: When such rotations accompany observer translation, the rotational velocity patterns must be discounted to accurately perceive heading.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of visual perception during self-motion.

claim: The conventional view holds that discounting rotations requires efference copies of self-generated eye/head movements.
source: The conventional view holds that this computation requires efference copies of self-generated eye/head movements.
evidence: This refers to established views in the field, which are later cited in the introduction.

claim: The brain implements an alternative solution in which retinal velocity patterns are themselves used to dissociate translations from rotations.
source: Here we demonstrate that the brain implements an alternative solution in which retinal velocity patterns are themselves used to dissociate translations from rotations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: The visual system utilizes both local motion parallax cues and global perspective distortions to estimate heading in the presence of rotations.
source: Specifically, we show that the visual system utilizes both local motion parallax cues and global perspective distortions to estimate heading in the presence of rotations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing 3D cloud and fronto-parallel plane stimuli.

claim: The brain is capable of performing complex computations to infer eye movements and discount their sensory consequences based solely on visual cues.
source: These findings further suggest that the brain is capable of performing complex computations to infer eye movements and discount their sensory consequences based solely on visual cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, particularly from simulated pursuit conditions.

claim: Retinal images of the environment are altered by self-generated rotations such as eye or head movements.
source: Retinal images of the environment are altered by self-generated rotations such as eye or head movements.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual perception.

claim: The component of retinal patterns resulting from rotations needs to be discounted by the visual system to perceive the world accurately.
source: In order to perceive the world accurately, the component of retinal patterns resulting from such rotations needs to be discounted by the visual system.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of visual perception.

claim: How the brain achieves rotation-invariant visual representation of the world remains unclear.
source: How the brain achieves such a rotation-invariant visual representation of the world remains unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Achieving rotation-invariance is critical for accurate behavior during visually guided navigation.
source: Visually guided navigation is an important context in which achieving rotation-invariance is critical for accurate behavior (Gibson, 1950; Warren and Saunders, 1995; Grigo and Lappe, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Self-motion results in retinal velocity patterns known as 'optic flow'.
source: Self-motion results in retinal velocity patterns known as 'optic flow' (Gibson, 1950).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Gibson (1950).

claim: During translations, the resulting retinal pattern is generally an expansionary or contractionary radial flow field from which the FOE can be used to estimate heading.
source: During translations, the resulting retinal pattern is generally an expansionary or contractionary radial flow field from which the point of zero velocity (Focus of Expansion, FOE) can be used to estimate heading (Tanaka et al., 1986; Warren et al., 1988; Duffy and Wurtz, 1995; Britten, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Eye or head rotations alter the optic flow pattern such that deciphering heading requires decomposing the resultant optic flow into translational and rotational components.
source: However, eye or head rotations alter this flow pattern such that deciphering heading requires decomposing the resultant optic flow into translational and rotational components (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated by Figure 1A.

claim: Psychophysical and electrophysiological studies have often emphasized the role of non-visual signals, such as efference copies, in discounting rotations to estimate heading.
source: Psychophysical (Royden et al., 1992; Royden, 1994; Crowell et al., 1998) and electrophysiological (Bradley et al., 1996; Page and Duffy, 1999; Zhang et al., 2004) studies have often emphasized the role of non-visual signals, such as efference copies of self-generated eye/head movements, in discounting rotations to estimate heading.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Non-visual signals can represent several different sources of rotation, including eye-in-head (REH), head-on-body (RHB), and body-in-world (RBW) movements.
source: Such non-visual signals can represent several different sources of rotation, including eye-in-head (REH), head-on-body (RHB), and body-in-world (RBW) movements (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Retinal image motion is determined by the translation and rotation of the eye relative to the world (TEW and REW).
source: Critically, retinal image motion is determined by the translation and rotation of the eye relative to the world (TEW and REW, Figure 1B)
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Extracting heading from optic flow requires compensating for the total rotation of the eye-in-world (REW = REH + RHB + RBW).
source: such that extracting heading from optic flow requires compensating for the total rotation of the eye-in-world (where, REW = REH + RHB + RBW).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between different rotation sources.

claim: Multiple non-visual signals would need to be added to achieve a rotation-invariant estimate of heading, potentially compounding the noise associated with each signal.
source: Therefore, in general, multiple non-visual signals would need to be added to achieve a rotation-invariant estimate of heading, potentially compounding the noise that is associated with each signal (Gellman and Fletcher, 1992; Li and Matin, 1992; Crowell et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations about signal noise.

claim: Rotation-invariance can theoretically be achieved exclusively through visual processing.
source: Alternatively, rotation-invariance can theoretically be achieved exclusively through visual processing (Longuet-Higgins and Prazdny, 1980; Rieger and Lawton, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: If the brain can use optic flow to directly estimate and discount rotations of the eye-in-world (REW), such mechanisms may provide a complementary and potentially more efficient way to decompose rotations and translations.
source: If the brain can use optic flow to directly estimate and discount rotations of the eye-in-world (REW), such mechanisms may provide a complementary and potentially more efficient way to decompose rotations and translations to achieve invariant heading perception.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Psychophysical studies have provided evidence that visual cues may play a role in estimating heading in the presence of rotations.
source: Psychophysical studies have provided evidence that visual cues may play a role in estimating heading in the presence of rotations (Grigo and Lappe, 1999; Li and Warren, 2000; Crowell and Andersen, 2001; Li and Warren, 2002, 2004; Royden et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to psychophysical studies.

claim: Electrophysiological evidence for the role of visual cues is ambiguous because previous studies either did not include visual controls for eye rotation, simulated rotations incorrectly, or employed insufficient analysis methods.
source: However, electrophysiological evidence for the role of visual cues is ambiguous, in part because previous neurophysiological studies either did not include visual controls for eye rotation (Zhang et al., 2004), simulated rotations incorrectly (Bradley et al., 1996; Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002) or employed insufficient analysis methods (Bradley et al., 1996; Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002; Bremmer et al., 2010; Kaminiarz et al., 2014) (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies supported by citations.

claim: A subpopulation of VIP neurons utilizes visual cues to signal heading in a rotation-invariant fashion.
source: Our results provide novel evidence that (1) a subpopulation of VIP neurons utilizes visual cues to signal heading in a rotation-invariant fashion
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Both local motion parallax and global perspective cues present in optic flow contribute to rotation-invariant heading computations in VIP.
source: and (2) both local motion parallax and global perspective cues present in optic flow contribute to these computations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing different stimulus types.

claim: Visual and non-visual sources of rotation elicit similar responses in VIP, suggesting multi-sensory combination of both visual and non-visual cues in representing rotations.
source: In addition, we find that visual and non-visual sources of rotation elicit similar responses in VIP, suggesting multi-sensory combination of both visual and non-visual cues in representing rotations.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data showing correlations between responses.

claim: Rotation-invariance is distinct from the reference frame used to represent heading.
source: We further show that rotation-invariance is distinct from the reference frame used to represent heading
evidence: This is a finding supported by analysis of temporal response dynamics.

claim: Heading representation in VIP is close to eye-centered.
source: and provide additional support that heading representation in VIP is close to eye-centered (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data and consistent with previous work.

claim: When rotation and translation occur simultaneously, adding rotation results in different FOE shifts at different depths in a visual scene with depth structure.
source: However, in a visual scene with depth structure, adding rotation results in different FOE shifts at different depths (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Zhang et al., 2004.

claim: The magnitudes of translational optic flow vectors decrease with distance (depth), whereas rotational optic flow vectors are independent of depth.
source: This is due to a key difference in the properties of optic flow resulting from translations and rotations—the magnitudes of translational optic flow vectors decrease with distance (depth), whereas rotational optic flow vectors are independent of depth (Longuet-Higgins and Prazdny, 1980).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Longuet-Higgins and Prazdny, 1980.

claim: For the translation and rotation parameters used in this study, the nearest plane in the 3D cloud (25 cm) results in an FOE shift of approximately 20°.
source: For the translation and rotation parameters used in this study, the nearest plane in the 3D cloud (25 cm) results in an FOE shift of approximately 20°.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental parameters.

claim: For any plane farther than 45 cm in the 3D cloud stimulus, the resultant optic flow has an undefined FOE.
source: However, for any plane farther than 45 cm, the resultant optic flow has an undefined FOE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, top row).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 based on the stimulus parameters.

claim: The simulated 3D cloud ranged from 25 cm to 125 cm, resulting in a large volume of the stimulus space having undefined FOE shifts.
source: The simulated 3D cloud ranged from 25 cm to 125 cm, resulting in a large volume of the stimulus space having undefined FOE shifts.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: Forward translations result in an expansionary flow field, and adding a rightward rotation causes a rightward shift of the focus of expansion.
source: Forward translations result in an expansionary flow field, for which adding a rightward rotation causes a rightward shift of the focus of expansion (for any given plane).
evidence: This is established knowledge about optic flow properties.

claim: Backward translations produce a contractionary flow field and adding a rightward rotation results in a leftward shift in the focus of contraction.
source: On the other hand, backward translations produce a contractionary flow field and adding a rightward rotation results in a leftward shift in the focus of contraction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: If a neuron signals heading regardless of the presence of rotations, then its tuning curves during real and simulated pursuit should be identical to the heading tuning curve measured during pure translation.
source: If a neuron signals heading regardless of the presence of rotations, then its tuning curves during real and simulated pursuit should be identical to the heading tuning curve measured during pure translation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: For a neuron that represents the resultant optic flow rather than the translation component, a transformation of the tuning curve is expected due to the added rotations.
source: For a neuron that instead represents the resultant optic flow rather than the translation component (heading), a transformation of the tuning curve is expected due to the added rotations.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on optic flow properties.

claim: The expected effect of rotation on heading tuning is not simply a global shift of the tuning curve, as was assumed previously.
source: Therefore, under the null hypothesis that neural responses are simply determined by the resultant optic flow, the expected effect of rotation on heading tuning is not simply a global shift of the tuning curve, as was assumed previously (Bradley et al., 1996; Page and Duffy, 1999; Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002; Bremmer et al., 2010; Kaminiarz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a critical insight about previous assumptions, supported by theoretical analysis.

claim: The example neuron in Figure 3A signals heading in a manner that is largely invariant to eye rotation during real pursuit.
source: The tuning curves in this example show only minor changes during RP indicating that the cell signals heading in a manner that is largely invariant to eye rotation, consistent with previous findings for real eye rotation (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 3A and consistent with previous findings.

claim: The tuning curves of the example neuron in Figure 3A during simulated pursuit also change very little, showcasing the role of visual signals in compensating for rotation.
source: Interestingly, the tuning curves of the same neuron during SP also change very little, showcasing the role of visual signals in compensating for rotation.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Rotation invariance in VIP that was previously attributed to non-visual signals might also be driven by visual cues.
source: Thus, rotation invariance in VIP that was previously attributed to non-visual signals (Zhang et al., 2004) might also be driven by visual cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from the example neuron and comparison to previous work.

claim: Bandwidth changes were observed consistently among VIP neurons that preferred lateral translations.
source: Such bandwidth changes were observed consistently among VIP neurons that preferred lateral translations; specifically, rightward rotations increased bandwidth for cells preferring rightward headings (∼0°) and decreased bandwidth for cells preferring leftward headings (∼180°), with the opposite pattern holding for leftward rotations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of the effects of rotation on heading tuning requires more complex and rigorous approaches than the cross-correlation or rank-order methods used in previous studies.
source: Because of these changes in tuning curve bandwidth or shape, analysis of the effects of rotation on heading tuning requires more complex and rigorous approaches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) than the cross-correlation or rank-order methods used in previous studies (Bradley et al., 1996; Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002; Bremmer et al., 2010; Kaminiarz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is critical to distinguish between changes in response gain and changes in the shape of tuning curves.
source: It is also critical to distinguish between changes in response gain and changes in the shape (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; see Discussion) of tuning curves, which our analysis allows because we sample the entire heading tuning curve (Mullette-Gillman et al., 2009; Chang and Snyder, 2010; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 22/72 (30.6%) neurons showed shifts that were not significantly different from zero during real pursuit, indicating rotation-invariant heading representation.
source: In the RP condition, 22/72 (30.6%) neurons showed shifts that were not significantly different from zero (bootstrap 95% CI); these cells can be considered to represent heading in a rotation-invariant fashion.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: 17/72 (23.6%) neurons had shifts that were not significantly different from zero during simulated pursuit, indicating that purely visual cues were sufficient to achieve rotation-invariance.
source: For SP, 17/72 (23.6%) neurons had shifts that were not significantly different from zero, indicating that purely visual cues were sufficient to achieve rotation-invariance in these neurons.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: Only 13/72 (18.1%) neurons during real pursuit and 19/72 (23.4%) neurons during simulated pursuit showed shifts significantly greater than 20°, suggesting that only a minority of VIP neurons simply represent the resultant optic flow.
source: Only 13/72 (18.1%) neurons during RP and 19/72 (23.4%) neurons during SP showed shifts that were significantly greater than 20°, suggesting that only a minority of VIP neurons simply represent the resultant optic flow.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: The median shift of the population during real pursuit is 8.5°, which is significantly less than the 13.8° median shift observed during simulated pursuit.
source: The median shift of the population during RP is 8.5°, which is significantly less than the 13.8° median shift observed during SP (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; p = 0.02), indicating greater tolerance to rotations in the presence of both non-visual and visual cues.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: Both median shifts (real and simulated pursuit) are significantly greater than 0° and less than 20°, suggesting that VIP neurons do not simply represent the resultant optic flow, but rather signal heading in a manner that is at least partially tolerant to rotations.
source: However, both median shifts are significantly greater than 0° (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; p < 0.001), and less than 20° (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; RP: p < 0.001, SP: p = 0.005) suggesting that, on average, VIP neurons do not simply represent the resultant optic flow, but rather signal heading in a manner that is at least partially tolerant to rotations.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: VIP can signal heading in the presence of rotations using both visual and non-visual cues.
source: Together, these findings indicate that VIP can signal heading in the presence of rotations using both visual and non-visual cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Tolerance to rotations is observed even when only visual cues are present (simulated pursuit).
source: Importantly, this tolerance to rotations is observed even when only visual cues are present (SP).
evidence: This is a key finding based on the simulated pursuit data.

claim: Previous studies have shown that VIP receives efference copies of pursuit eye movements, reflecting an REH signal.
source: Previous studies have shown that VIP receives efference copies of pursuit eye movements (Colby et al., 1993; Duhamel et al., 1997), reflecting an REH signal.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: About half of the rotation responses were significantly different from baseline activity during both real and simulated rotations (73/144, 50.7% during pursuit in darkness and 78/144, 54.2% during simulated rotation).
source: We found that about half of the rotation responses were significantly different from baseline activity during both real and simulated rotations (144 responses from 72 cells; 73/144, 50.7% during pursuit in darkness and 78/144, 54.2% during simulated rotation).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: The baseline-subtracted responses to real and simulated rotation stimuli are significantly correlated (rightward rotation: Spearman r = 0.50, p < 0.001; leftward rotation: Spearman r = 0.39; p = 0.001).
source: We find that the baseline-subtracted responses to these two types of rotation stimuli are significantly correlated (rightward rotation: Spearman r = 0.50, p < 0.001; leftward rotation: Spearman r = 0.39; p = 0.001), supporting the presence of a rotation signal derived from purely visual cues (REW) in area VIP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many VIP neurons exhibit direction-selective responses to rotation.
source: Furthermore, the difference in response between rightward and leftward rotations (Figure 5B) shows that many VIP neurons exhibit direction-selective responses to rotation.
evidence: This is a finding based on data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is significant correlation between the differential responses (left—right rotation) during real and simulated rotation (Spearman r = 0.59; p < 0.001).
source: We also find significant correlation between the differential responses (left—right rotation) during real and simulated rotation (Spearman r = 0.59; p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: The correlations observed support the hypothesis of multi-sensory convergence of visual and non-visual cues to provide consistent rotation information.
source: These results support the hypothesis of multi-sensory convergence of visual and non-visual cues to provide consistent rotation information, which may be critical for encoding rotations, in addition to achieving a rotation-invariant representation of heading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: In a 3D environment, two points can have similar retinal locations, but different depths, and optic flow vectors resulting from observer translation are dependent on depth, producing different retinal velocities for points at different depths.
source: In a 3D environment, two points can have similar retinal locations, but different depths. As illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, optic flow vectors resulting from observer translation are dependent on depth, producing different retinal velocities for points at different depths.
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rotations produce image motion that is not depth-dependent, and therefore lacking local motion parallax.
source: Rotations, on the other hand, produce image motion that is not depth-dependent, and therefore lacking local motion parallax.
evidence: This is established knowledge about optic flow properties.

claim: For a rich 3D environment, computing the local difference between optic flow vectors corresponding to points at different depths allows the rotational component of optic flow to be subtracted away.
source: As a result, for a rich 3D environment, computing the local difference between optic flow vectors corresponding to points at different depths allows the rotational component of optic flow to be subtracted away (Longuet-Higgins and Prazdny, 1980; Rieger and Lawton, 1985; Warren and Hannon, 1990)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from theoretical work.

claim: The singularity point of the motion parallax field corresponds to the observer's heading.
source: and the singularity point of the resulting motion parallax field (Figure 6A) corresponds to the observer's heading.
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Optic flow contains global components of motion that convey information about observer rotation, independent of the depth structure of the scene.
source: In addition to local motion parallax cues resulting from observer translation, optic flow also contains global components of motion that convey information about observer rotation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about optic flow properties.

claim: A correct simulation of rotational optic flow can be characterized as a combination of laminar flow and dynamic perspective cues.
source: A correct simulation of rotational optic flow can thus be characterized as a combination of laminar flow and dynamic perspective cues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a methodological claim illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Dynamic perspective cues are independent of the depth structure of the scene and are present in scenes having rich 3D structure as well as scenes consisting of a single plane.
source: Importantly, these cues are independent of the depth structure of the scene and are present in scenes having rich 3D structure as well as scenes consisting of a single plane.
evidence: This is a property of dynamic perspective cues.

claim: Theoretical studies have proposed that dynamic perspective cues may play an important role in estimating and discounting the rotational component of optic flow to estimate heading.
source: Theoretical studies have proposed that such cues may play an important role in estimating and discounting the rotational component of optic flow to estimate heading (Koenderink and van Doorn, 1976, 1981; Grigo and Lappe, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: A recent electrophysiological study in MT provides evidence that the visual system may be capable of using dynamic perspective cues to disambiguate the sign of depth specified by motion parallax.
source: A recent electrophysiological study in MT provides evidence that the visual system may be capable of using these dynamic perspective cues to disambiguate the sign of depth specified by motion parallax (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: During the middle 750 ms of a forward translation stimulus with the fronto-parallel plane, real or simulated pursuit results in an average FOE shift of 37°.
source: During the middle 750 ms of a forward translation stimulus, real or simulated pursuit results in an average FOE shift of 37°.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental parameters for the FP stimulus.

claim: The median shifts across the population for real pursuit (14.3°) and simulated pursuit (21.5°) with the fronto-parallel plane stimulus were both significantly less than the 37° expected if there were no tolerance for rotations.
source: The median shifts across the population for real pursuit (14.3°) and simulated pursuit (21.5°) were both significantly less than the 37° expected if there were no tolerance for rotations (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; p < 0.005).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: 8/34 (23.5%) neurons during real pursuit and 5/34 (14.7%) neurons during simulated pursuit with the fronto-parallel plane had shifts that were not significantly different from 0°, implying rotation-invariant heading responses.
source: Furthermore, 8/34 (23.5%) neurons during RP and 5/34 (14.7%) neurons during SP had shifts that were not significantly different from 0° (darker colors in Figure 6C), implying rotation-invariant heading responses.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only 6/34 (17.6%) neurons during real pursuit and 12/34 (35.3%) neurons during simulated pursuit with the fronto-parallel plane showed shifts that were statistically greater than or not different from 37°.
source: Only 6/34 (17.6%) neurons during RP and 12/34 (35.3%) neurons during SP showed shifts that were statistically greater than or not different from 37° (95% CI; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the recorded data.

claim: Even in the absence of non-visual signals and 3D visual cues such as local motion parallax, a large sub-population of VIP neurons can use global perspective cues to at least partially mitigate the effect of rotations on heading tuning.
source: These results indicate that, even in the absence of non-visual signals and 3D visual cues such as local motion parallax, a large sub-population of VIP neurons can use global perspective cues to at least partially mitigate the effect of rotations on heading tuning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fronto-parallel plane experimental findings.

claim: Shifts measured during simulated pursuit in the 3D cloud experiments were significantly less than shifts measured using the fronto-parallel plane.
source: Shifts measured during simulated pursuit in the 3D cloud experiments were significantly less than shifts measured using the FP plane (Wilcoxon rank sum test; p = 0.02).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical comparison between the two experimental conditions.

claim: Both local motion parallax cues arising from translations, and global features such as dynamic perspective cues arising from rotations play important roles in visually dissociating translations and rotations.
source: This implies that both local motion parallax cues arising from translations, and global features such as dynamic perspective cues arising from rotations play important roles in visually dissociating translations and rotations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the 3D cloud and fronto-parallel plane results.

claim: Previous studies interpreted rotation-invariant heading tuning as evidence that VIP neurons represent self-motion in a head-centered reference frame.
source: Since the eyes physically rotate during real pursuit, but the head does not, previous studies interpreted rotation-invariant heading tuning as evidence that VIP neurons represent self-motion in a head-centered reference frame (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of previous interpretations cited from Zhang et al., 2004.

claim: Studies that measured heading tuning with the eye and head at different static positions have revealed an eye-centered reference frame for visual heading tuning in VIP.
source: In contrast, studies that measured heading tuning with the eye and head at different static positions have revealed an eye-centered reference frame for visual heading tuning in VIP (Chen et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The issues of rotation-invariant heading tuning and reference frames are not necessarily linked.
source: However, we posit that the issues of rotation-invariant heading tuning and reference frames are not necessarily linked.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that the study aims to demonstrate.

claim: VIP neurons can discount rotations without signaling translation direction in a head-centered reference frame.
source: Indeed, we show below that VIP neurons can discount rotations without signaling translation direction in a head-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is a finding that will be supported by subsequent analysis.

claim: During eye pursuit, the eye-centered reference frame rotates relative to a subject's heading.
source: The key to reconciling these issues is appreciating that, during eye pursuit, the eye-centered reference frame rotates relative to a subject's heading (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a theoretical insight illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: As the eye rotates, the direction of translation remains constant in head-centered coordinates.
source: As the eye rotates, the direction of translation remains constant in head-centered coordinates (Figure 7A, dashed green lines).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: In the rotating eye-centered reference frame, the translation direction relative to the eye changes over time, such that the focus of expansion moves across the retina.
source: However, in the rotating eye-centered reference frame, the translation direction relative to the eye changes over time, such that the focus of expansion moves across the retina (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: The temporal change in the translation direction with respect to the retina is the same during both real and simulated pursuit.
source: Hence, the temporal change in the translation direction with respect to the retina is the same during both real and simulated pursuit.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design.

claim: Time-averaged neural responses may provide insight into what signal is represented (heading or resultant optic flow), but not about whether these signals are represented in an eye- or head-centered reference frame.
source: Therefore, the average eye position is the same as the average head position. As a result, time-averaged neural responses may provide insight into what signal is represented (heading or resultant optic flow), but not about whether these signals are represented in an eye- or head-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is a methodological insight about the limitations of time-averaged responses.

claim: An eye-centered representation of heading would result in systematic temporal response variations due to the rotating reference frame, and these variations would be different for leftward and rightward rotations of the eye.
source: Accordingly, an eye-centered representation of heading would result in systematic temporal response variations due to the rotating reference frame, and these variations would be different for leftward and rightward rotations of the eye.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about temporal response patterns.

claim: A head-centered representation would result in responses that are constant over time, and similar for rightward and leftward rotations during both real and simulated pursuit.
source: In contrast, a head-centered representation would result in responses that are constant over time, and similar for rightward and leftward rotations during both real and simulated pursuit.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about temporal response patterns.

claim: For a neuron representing heading in an eye-centered reference frame, a rightward eye rotation would result in an upward trend in firing rate over time for headings along the positive slope of the tuning curve, while a leftward eye rotation would result in a downward trend.
source: For a neuron representing heading in an eye-centered reference frame, a rightward eye rotation would result in an upward trend in firing rate over time for headings along the positive slope of the tuning curve. In contrast, a leftward eye rotation would result in a downward trend (Figure 7C,D, dashed lines).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The temporal trends in firing rate are determined by the changing eye position and are independent of how tolerant the heading representation is to rotations.
source: It is important to note that these trends are determined by the changing eye position and are independent of how tolerant the heading representation is to rotations (i.e., the extent of compensation).
evidence: This is a theoretical insight about the independence of reference frame and rotation compensation.

claim: Neurons can represent translations invariant to rotations in either a head-centered or an eye-centered reference frame.
source: Therefore, neurons can represent translations invariant to rotations in either a head-centered or an eye-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion about the independence of rotation invariance and reference frame.

claim: VIP population responses show trends in the directions predicted by an eye-centered reference frame, but are inconsistent with the expectation for a head-centered reference frame.
source: VIP population responses show trends in the directions predicted by an eye-centered reference frame, but are inconsistent with the expectation for a head-centered reference frame (red, blue curves in Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of temporal response dynamics shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The slopes observed in VIP responses correspond to an intermediate reference frame that lies closer to an eye-centered frame than a head-centered reference frame.
source: The slopes observed in VIP responses correspond to an intermediate reference frame that lies closer to an eye-centered frame than a head-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is a finding based on quantitative analysis of the temporal response slopes.

claim: For real pursuit, average responses increased for rightward eye rotation (slope = 0.29/s, 95% CI = [0.21 0.37]) and decreased for leftward rotation (slope = −0.24/s, 95% CI = [−0.16–0.32]).
source: Specifically, for real pursuit, average responses increased for rightward eye rotation (slope = 0.29/s, 95% CI = [0.21 0.37], linear regression) and decreased for leftward rotation (slope = −0.24/s, 95% CI = [−0.16–0.32]).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of temporal response dynamics.

claim: The slopes during real pursuit are significantly different from 0 and ∼65% as steep as the predictions of the eye-centered reference frame, thus indicating an intermediate reference frame.
source: These slopes are significantly different from 0 and ∼65% as steep as the predictions of the eye-centered reference frame, thus indicating an intermediate reference frame.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of observed slopes to theoretical predictions.

claim: Similar temporal trends are observed during simulated pursuit (rightward: slope = 0.28/s, 95% CI = [0.21 0.35]; leftward: slope = −0.26/s, 95% CI = [−0.17–0.35]).
source: Interestingly, similar trends are also observed during simulated pursuit (rightward: slope = 0.28/s, 95% CI = [0.21 0.35]; leftward: slope = −0.26/s, 95% CI = [−0.17–0.35], linear regression), for which the eye does not physically rotate.
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of temporal response dynamics during simulated pursuit.

claim: Visual signals in VIP carry information about changes in eye position even in the absence of efference copy signals.
source: Whereas previous studies have demonstrated a role of non-visual signals in estimating the position of the eye or head relative to the body (Squatrito and Maioli, 1997; Lewis et al., 1998; Klier et al., 2005), these results suggest that visual signals in VIP carry information about changes in eye position even in the absence of efference copy signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulated pursuit findings, contrasted with previous work.

claim: The temporal dynamics of an eye rotation may be inferred from the rotational components of optic flow and used to modulate neural responses during simulated pursuit.
source: In other words, the temporal dynamics of an eye rotation may be inferred from the rotational components of optic flow and used to modulate neural responses during simulated pursuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how visual signals might produce the observed temporal dynamics.

claim: A sub-population of VIP neurons represent heading in a rotation-invariant fashion while a majority of the population is at least partially tolerant to rotations.
source: We evaluated how heading is represented in macaque area VIP in the presence of rotations, finding that a sub-population of VIP neurons represent heading in a rotation-invariant fashion while a majority of the population is at least partially tolerant to rotations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Rotation invariance can be achieved using both non-visual and purely visual cues.
source: Importantly, rotation invariance can be achieved using both non-visual and purely visual cues.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: Previous neurophysiology literature emphasized the importance of non-visual cues, especially efference copy signals, but clear evidence for the role of visual cues has been missing.
source: Previous neurophysiology literature emphasized the importance of non-visual cues, especially efference copy signals, but clear evidence for the role of visual cues has been missing, as discussed below.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the literature.

claim: The significant correlation between visual and non-visual rotation responses is consistent with a multi-sensory representation of rotations.
source: The significant correlation between visual and non-visual rotation responses is consistent with a multi-sensory representation of rotations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: Rotation tolerance does not necessarily imply a head-centered reference frame.
source: Specifically, we examine the effect of a rotating eye reference frame on visual responses to show that rotation tolerance does not necessarily imply a head-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is a key conceptual finding of the study.

claim: Visual cues play a significant role in achieving rotation-invariant heading representations.
source: Our findings show conclusively that visual cues play a significant role in achieving rotation-invariant heading representations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The significance of visual cues in discounting rotation extends beyond eye pursuit to head-on-body (RHB) and body-in-world (RBW) rotations as well.
source: It is important to recognize that the significance of visual cues in discounting rotation extends beyond eye pursuit to head-on-body (RHB) and body-in-world (RBW) rotations as well.
evidence: This is a generalization of the findings beyond the specific experimental conditions.

claim: If eye, head, and body rotations are generated simultaneously, multiple efference copy signals must be added together and subsequently discounted from the resultant optic flow to signal heading accurately.
source: If we consider that eye, head, and body rotations are often generated simultaneously, multiple efference copy signals must be added together and subsequently discounted from the resultant optic flow to signal heading accurately.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the complexity of using efference copy signals.

claim: Each efference copy signal is associated with signal-dependent noise; thus, combining multiple, potentially independent, efference copy signals to estimate rotations may not always be an efficient solution for the brain.
source: Each of these non-visual signals is associated with signal-dependent noise (Gellman and Fletcher, 1992; Li and Matin, 1992; Crowell et al., 1998); thus, combining multiple, potentially independent, efference copy signals to estimate rotations may not always be an efficient solution for the brain.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations about signal noise.

claim: The information contained in visual cues is independent of the source of rotation and represents rotation of the eye relative to the world (REW).
source: On the other hand, the information contained in visual cues is independent of the source of rotation and represents rotation of the eye relative to the world (REW).
evidence: This is a theoretical insight about the nature of visual rotation information.

claim: The REW information present in optic flow inherently reflects the sum of all the different sources of rotation (REW = REH + RHB + RBW) and thus provides direct information regarding the total rotation of the eyes during self-motion.
source: The REW information present in optic flow inherently reflects the sum of all the different sources of rotation (REW = REH + RHB + RBW) and thus provides direct information regarding the total rotation of the eyes during self-motion.
evidence: This is a theoretical insight about the advantages of visual rotation information.

claim: Visual signals may have important advantages when the goal is to accurately estimate heading in the presence of self-generated rotations.
source: Therefore, visual signals may have important advantages when the goal is to accurately estimate heading in the presence of self-generated rotations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the theoretical advantages of visual signals.

claim: Non-visual signals may be crucial in situations where visual information may be sparse, such as driving at night on an open road.
source: However, we also face situations in which visual information may be sparse, such as driving at night on an open road (limited visual range and depth structure), where non-visual signals may be crucial.
evidence: This is a speculation about when non-visual signals would be important.

claim: Both visual and non-visual signals contribute to discounting rotations to represent heading.
source: As expected, given the brain's propensity towards multi-sensory integration, we find that both visual and non-visual signals contribute to discounting rotations to represent heading.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Real pursuit shifts are smaller than simulated pursuit shifts, and both types of shifts are smaller for a dense 3D cloud than a fronto-parallel plane.
source: Real pursuit shifts are smaller than simulated pursuit shifts, and both types of shifts are smaller for a dense 3D cloud than a fronto-parallel plane.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative findings across conditions.

claim: VIP contains an integrated representation of rotation that relies on both visual signals and efference copy inputs.
source: Given the variety of efference copy signals present in parietal cortex (Andersen, 1997) and the correlation observed between the REH (pursuit in darkness) and REW (pure simulated rotation) responses in our data (Figure 5), we postulate that VIP contains an integrated representation of rotation that relies on both visual signals and efference copy inputs.
evidence: This is a postulate based on the data and previous knowledge.

claim: Some psychophysical studies report large errors in heading perception in the absence of efference copy signals when using 3D cloud stimuli.
source: If we consider studies that used 3D cloud stimuli, we find that some studies report large errors in heading perception (the difference between reported heading and true heading) in the absence of efference copy signals (Royden et al., 1992; Royden, 1994; Banks et al., 1996)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited psychophysical studies.

claim: Other psychophysical studies report that subjects are able to accurately perceive their heading based on purely visual stimuli.
source: whereas other studies report that subjects are able to accurately perceive their heading based on purely visual stimuli (Warren and Hannon, 1988, 1990; van den Berg and Brenner, 1994).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited psychophysical studies.

claim: The rotation compensation observed in psychophysical studies during simulated pursuit (only visual cues) ranged from 100% to 20% for a 3D cloud stimulus.
source: The rotation compensation observed in these studies during simulated pursuit (only visual cues) ranged from 100% to 20% for a 3D cloud stimulus (based on the depth plane corresponding to the screen distance).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from psychophysical studies.

claim: Studies with smaller compensatory effects used visual stimuli with a small field of view and a low density of dots in the 3D cloud, thus limiting the visual information available for estimating heading in the presence of rotations.
source: Studies with smaller compensatory effects (Royden et al., 1992; Royden, 1994; Banks et al., 1996) concluded that optic flow was insufficient for estimating translations in the presence of rotations. However, these studies used visual stimuli with a small field of view and a low density of dots in the 3D cloud, thus limiting the visual information available for estimating heading in the presence of rotations (Grigo and Lappe, 1999).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Other studies have shown that richer visual stimuli, including landmarks and larger fields of view, resulted in larger compensatory effects based on purely visual cues.
source: Moreover, other studies have shown that richer visual stimuli, including landmarks (Li and Warren, 2000, 2004; Royden et al., 2006) and larger fields of view (van den Berg and Brenner, 1994; Grigo and Lappe, 1999), resulted in larger compensatory effects based on purely visual cues.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited psychophysical studies.

claim: Using a 3D cloud stimulus, a large and continuous range of compensatory effects was observed, including a substantial subset of VIP neurons that compensated completely for rotations, as well as neurons that do not compensate at all or even over-compensate for rotations.
source: In this study, using a 3D cloud stimulus, we observed a large and continuous range of compensatory effects, including a substantial subset of VIP neurons that compensated completely for rotations, as well as neurons that do not compensate at all or even over-compensate for rotations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The fact that moderate, but significant, compensation was found during simulated pursuit is broadly consistent with the psychophysical literature.
source: However, the fact that we find moderate, but significant, compensation during simulated pursuit is broadly consistent with the psychophysical literature.
evidence: This is a comparison of the findings to the psychophysical literature.

claim: Depending on how the population of VIP neurons is decoded, a substantial range of behavioral effects might be expected.
source: Furthermore, depending on how the population of VIP neurons is decoded, a substantial range of behavioral effects might be expected.
evidence: This is a speculation about how neural responses might relate to behavior.

claim: Some psychophysical studies attribute the errors observed during simulated pursuit to the misinterpretation of path-independent rotations as motion along a curved path.
source: Some psychophysical studies attribute the errors observed during simulated pursuit to the misinterpretation of path-independent rotations (such as eye pursuit during straight translations) as motion along a curved path (Royden, 1994; Royden et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a summary of interpretations from cited psychophysical studies.

claim: In behavioral studies that eliminate the ambiguity between path-independent rotations and curved paths through specific instruction to subjects, heading errors during simulated pursuit are reported to be largely reduced.
source: In behavioral studies that eliminate this ambiguity through specific instruction to subjects, heading errors during simulated pursuit are reported to be largely reduced (Li and Warren, 2004; Royden et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited behavioral studies.

claim: The range of compensation observed in the data could be a result of the perceptual ambiguity between path-independent rotations and curved paths.
source: It is also possible that the range of compensation observed in our data could be a result of this perceptual ambiguity.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible explanation for the findings.

claim: Some previous studies did not use a simulated pursuit condition and therefore could not disambiguate visual and non-visual contributions to the rotation-invariance of heading tuning they observed.
source: Some studies did not use a simulated pursuit condition and therefore could not disambiguate visual and non-visual contributions to the rotation-invariance of heading tuning they observed (Page and Duffy, 1999; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies.

claim: Bradley et al. (1996) and Shenoy et al. (1999, 2002) included a simulated pursuit condition in their experiments, but the visual stimulus used to simulate pursuit was incorrect.
source: On the other hand, Bradley et al. (1996) and Shenoy et al. (1999); (2002) included a simulated pursuit condition in their experiments, but the visual stimulus used to simulate pursuit was incorrect.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies.

claim: Bradley et al. (1996) and Shenoy et al. (1999, 2002) simply added laminar flow to their fronto-parallel plane optic flow stimuli to mimic pursuit, and thus their stimuli lacked the dynamic perspective cues necessary to accurately simulate eye rotations on a flat display.
source: To mimic pursuit, they simply added laminar flow to their fronto-parallel plane (i.e. no local motion parallax cues) optic flow stimuli, and thus their stimuli lacked the dynamic perspective cues necessary to accurately simulate eye rotations on a flat display.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the methods used in previous studies.

claim: When rendering visual stimuli, dynamic perspective cues should be incorporated any time the eye changes orientation relative to the scene.
source: When rendering visual stimuli, dynamic perspective cues should be incorporated any time the eye changes orientation relative to the scene (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation supported by citation.

claim: If eye rotation is simulated (incorrectly) as laminar flow on a flat screen, then it should not be possible for neurons to exhibit rotation-tolerant heading tuning because the addition of laminar motion simply shifts the focus of expansion in the flow field, and does not provide any rotation cues.
source: If eye rotation is simulated (incorrectly) as laminar flow on a flat screen, then it should not be possible for neurons to exhibit rotation-tolerant heading tuning because the addition of laminar motion simply shifts the focus of expansion in the flow field, and does not provide any rotation cues.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the consequences of incorrect stimulus simulation.

claim: Bradley et al. (1996) found that MSTd neurons did not compensate for rotations when pursuit was simulated as laminar flow.
source: Indeed, Bradley et al. (1996) found that MSTd neurons did not compensate for rotations when pursuit was simulated in this manner.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Shenoy et al. (1999, 2002) reported that MSTd neurons show considerable tolerance to rotation when pursuit was simulated as laminar flow, despite the fact that little or no rotation tolerance was reported psychophysically by the same laboratory for simulated pursuit.
source: In contrast, Shenoy et al. (1999); (2002) reported that MSTd neurons show considerable tolerance to rotation when pursuit was simulated as laminar flow, despite the fact that little or no rotation tolerance was reported psychophysically by the same laboratory for simulated pursuit (Crowell et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies and a noted inconsistency.

claim: Compared to Bradley et al. (1996), Shenoy et al. (2002) used a smaller display size and yet observed larger compensatory effects, which contradicts theoretical and psychophysical studies that have established that a larger display size should improve pursuit compensation based on visual cues.
source: Compared to Bradley et al. (1996), Shenoy et al. (2002) used a smaller display size and yet observed larger compensatory effects. This finding contradicts theoretical and psychophysical studies that have established that a larger display size should improve pursuit compensation based on visual cues (Koenderink and van Doorn, 1987; Grigo and Lappe, 1999).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies noting an inconsistency with theory.

claim: The counter-intuitive results obtained by Shenoy et al. (1999, 2002) stem from the fact that the boundary of their visual stimuli moved across the retina during real and simulated pursuit (but not during the fixation condition), and thus stimulated different regions of the visual field in and around the receptive field of a neuron over time.
source: We believe that the counter-intuitive results obtained by Shenoy et al. (1999); (2002) stem from the fact that the boundary of their visual stimuli moved across the retina during real and simulated pursuit (but not during the fixation condition), and thus stimulated different regions of the visual field in and around the receptive field of a neuron over time.
evidence: This is a critical assessment and proposed explanation for previous findings.

claim: Cross-correlation is invariant to gain changes, but only provides an accurate measure of tuning shifts if the tuning curve has a clear peak within the range of headings tested.
source: While cross-correlation is invariant to gain changes, it only provides an accurate measure of tuning shifts if the tuning curve has a clear peak within the range of headings tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a methodological insight illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells that prefer lateral headings generally have monotonic tuning curves around straight ahead, and this generally yields rather flat cross-correlation functions with no clear peak.
source: In contrast, cells that prefer lateral headings generally have monotonic tuning curves around straight ahead (e.g., Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), and this generally yields rather flat cross-correlation functions with no clear peak (e.g., Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a methodological insight illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis produces fairly accurate estimates of shifts for cells with heading preferences within the range of headings tested, but does not provide reliable shifts for neurons with monotonic tuning functions in that range.
source: As a result, cross-correlation analysis produces fairly accurate estimates of shifts for cells with heading preferences within the range of headings tested, but does not provide reliable shifts for neurons with monotonic tuning functions in that range (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is a methodological insight illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The degree of rotation compensation reported previously (Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002) may have been inaccurate for neurons with monotonic tuning around straight-forward, which are common in areas MSTd and VIP.
source: These simulations suggest that the degree of rotation compensation reported previously (Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002) may have been inaccurate for neurons with monotonic tuning around straight-forward, which are common in areas MSTd (Gu et al., 2006, 2010) and VIP (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies based on methodological insights.

claim: The partial rotation compensation observed by Shenoy et al. (1999, 2002) in their (incorrect) simulated rotation condition, which contained no relevant visual cues that could be used to compensate for rotation, may be explained by inaccuracies in the cross-correlation method.
source: This may also help explain the partial rotation compensation observed by Shenoy et al. (1999); (2002) in their (incorrect) simulated rotation condition, which contained no relevant visual cues that could be used to compensate for rotation.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for previous findings based on methodological insights.

claim: Bremmer et al. (2010) and Kaminiarz et al. (2014) reported that neurons in areas MSTd and VIP show rotation-invariant heading tuning based solely on visual cues.
source: More recently, Bremmer et al. (2010) and Kaminiarz et al. (2014) reported that neurons in areas MSTd and VIP, respectively, show rotation-invariant heading tuning based solely on visual cues.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Bremmer et al. (2010) and Kaminiarz et al. (2014) only measured neural responses to three headings and defined rotation-tolerance based on a rank-ordering of heading responses across the different eye movement conditions.
source: However, these studies only measured neural responses to three headings (forward, 30° leftward, and 30° rightward), and defined rotation-tolerance based on a rank-ordering of heading responses across the different eye movement conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in cited studies.

claim: Since absolute firing rates were not considered in the rank-ordering method, it is likely that shifts in tuning curves could go undetected in the presence of gain fields or bandwidth changes.
source: Since absolute firing rates were not considered, it is likely that shifts in tuning curves could go undetected by this method in the presence of gain fields or bandwidth changes.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the rank-ordering method.

claim: In the ground-plane stimuli used by Kaminiarz et al. (2014), rotation has a large effect on slow-speed optic flow vectors near the horizon, and high-speed foreground vectors are much less altered.
source: Consider that, in their ground-plane stimuli (e.g., Figure 1 of Kaminiarz et al., 2014), rotation has a large effect on slow-speed optic flow vectors near the horizon, and high-speed foreground vectors are much less altered.
evidence: This is an analysis of the stimulus properties used in a cited study.

claim: For neurons with receptive fields below the horizontal meridian or those with responses dominated by high speeds, one might not expect the rank ordering of heading responses to change even if neurons do not compensate for rotation.
source: For neurons with receptive fields below the horizontal meridian or those with responses dominated by high speeds, one might not expect the rank ordering of heading responses to change even if neurons do not compensate for rotation.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the rank-ordering method given the stimulus properties.

claim: The results of Bremmer et al. (2010) and Kaminiarz et al. (2014) are difficult to interpret.
source: Thus, the results of these studies are difficult to interpret.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies.

claim: The study accurately simulated eye rotations such that correct 2D and 3D visual cues are present in the stimuli.
source: By comparison with the above studies, we accurately simulated eye rotations such that correct 2D and 3D visual cues are present in the stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The study measured full heading tuning curves and the analysis methods allowed disambiguation of changes in response gain from shifts or shape changes in the tuning curve.
source: We also measured full heading tuning curves and our analysis methods allowed us to disambiguate changes in response gain from shifts or shape changes in the tuning curve.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: By using a large display and maintaining the same area of retinal stimulation for all viewing conditions, artifacts that likely confounded the results of some previous studies were eliminated.
source: By using a large display and maintaining the same area of retinal stimulation for all viewing conditions (see 'Materials and methods'), we eliminated artifacts that likely confounded the results of some previous studies (Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The findings in the simulated rotation condition reflect a true contribution of visual cues to the problem of dissociating translations and rotations.
source: Therefore, we are confident that our findings in the simulated rotation condition reflect a true contribution of visual cues to the problem of dissociating translations and rotations.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the validity of the findings.

claim: In order to navigate through the environment and interact successfully with objects, it is imperative that we distinguish visual motion caused by self-generated movements from that caused by external events in the world.
source: In order to navigate through the environment and interact successfully with objects, it is imperative that we distinguish visual motion caused by self-generated movements from that caused by external events in the world (Probst et al., 1984; Wallach, 1987; Warren and Saunders, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The visual consequences of eye or head rotations need to be discounted in order to accurately perceive whether an object is stationary or moving in the world.
source: For instance, the visual consequences of eye or head rotations need to be discounted in order to accurately perceive whether an object is stationary or moving in the world.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual perception.

claim: The neuroscience literature has extensively studied and emphasized the contribution of efference copy signals to discounting self-generated movements in several sensory systems.
source: The neuroscience literature has extensively studied and emphasized the contribution of efference copy signals to discounting self-generated movements in several sensory systems (Andersen, 1997; Cullen, 2004; Klier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a summary of the state of the literature supported by citations.

claim: The ability of VIP neurons to represent heading during rotations, even in the absence of efference copy signals, suggests that visual mechanisms may make substantial contributions to a variety of neural computations that involve estimating and accounting for self-generated rotations.
source: The ability of VIP neurons to represent heading during rotations, even in the absence of efference copy signals, suggests that visual mechanisms may make substantial contributions to a variety of neural computations that involve estimating and accounting for self-generated rotations.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings.

claim: The contribution of visual cues may be especially important in situations where efference copy signals are either unreliable or absent.
source: The contribution of visual cues may be especially important in situations where efference copy signals are either unreliable or absent.
evidence: This is a speculation about when visual cues would be particularly important.

claim: Driving along a winding path and looking in the direction of instantaneous heading does not result in any eye or head movements relative to the body (i.e., no efference copy signals), but such curvilinear motion still introduces rotational components in the optic flow field and disrupts the FOE.
source: For instance, driving along a winding path and looking in the direction of instantaneous heading does not result in any eye or head movements relative to the body (i.e., no efference copy signals). However, such curvilinear motion still introduces rotational components in the optic flow field and disrupts the FOE.
evidence: This is an example scenario illustrating when visual cues would be important.

claim: In order to estimate curvilinear motion trajectories, the visual system would need to decompose self-motion into both translational and rotational components.
source: In order to estimate such motion trajectories, the visual system would need to decompose self-motion into both translational and rotational components.
evidence: This is an inference about what would be required to estimate curvilinear motion.

claim: The study suggests that trajectory computations based purely on optic flow may be feasible.
source: This study suggests that such trajectory computations based purely on optic flow may be feasible.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.
